title: Hypercontractivity on a torus and juntas for Lipschitz functions
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: A complete proof of T. Austin's theorem that a function on the cube [0,1]^N with values in [-1,1] that is Lipschitz for the sup distance is within tau, in the mean square, of a function of at most J(L,tau) coordinates, with J independent of N. The first lesson gives the tools: trigonometric polynomials on a torus, Fejer means (approximation that keeps bounds and Lipschitz constants), the heat operators as Gaussian means, their action on characters, and three inequalities (Poincare; the heat operator moves a function slowly in L^1; a bound for the derivatives of P_t f in L^2). The second lesson proves a logarithmic Sobolev inequality on the circle, Ent(f^2) <= (7/4) |f'|_2^2, from a bound for the largest value of a function, an inequality with a defect, and Rothaus's lemma. The third lesson proves hypercontractivity of the heat operators on the circle by Gross's method (the norm |P_t f|_{q(t)} does not increase) and on a torus of any dimension by an induction that uses an inequality for mixed norms. The fourth lesson proves the junta theorem for trigonometric polynomials on a torus with an explicit bound, then for Lipschitz functions on a torus by Fejer means, then on the cube by a fold map. No hypothesis from the literature is used.
prerequisites: core course Measure and Integration (D10): the Lebesgue integral, Fubini's theorem, dominated convergence, the inequalities of Jensen, Hoelder and Cauchy-Schwarz
calculus of one and several variables (differentiation under the integral, integration by parts, the Gaussian integral)
the lessons prove every other fact they use

checks.reading: Written on 13 Oct 2026 to remove the named hypothesis (J) of the course large-independent-sets-in-three-colorable-graphs (OpenAI 106). Source for the plan of the proof: T. Austin, 'On the failure of concentration for the l-infinity ball', arXiv:1309.3315v4, pages 1 to 8 (Theorems 1.1, 1.2, 2.1; Lemma 2.2, Propositions 2.3 and 2.4, Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6; the proof of Theorem 2.1 with the passage to the cube). Every step was derived again. Where the course goes its own way: (1) Austin quotes the hypercontractive inequality for the heat semigroup on the circle from Weissler; the course proves a hypercontractive inequality with a weaker exponent from scratch: a logarithmic Sobolev inequality on the circle with the constant 7/4 (sup bound in one dimension, inequality with a defect, Rothaus's lemma with a proof by concavity that handles the logarithmic singularity through Fubini's theorem, Poincare inequality), then Gross's differentiation argument for positive trigonometric polynomials and an approximation by Fejer means, then tensorization by an inequality for mixed norms. (2) All differential arguments are carried out for trigonometric polynomials, where the heat operators act on finitely many Fourier coefficients; Lipschitz functions are reached by Fejer means, which keep the Lipschitz constant for the sup distance, the bounds and the means over coordinates. (3) The heat operators are normalized so that the heat equation is u_t = Laplace u (Gaussian of variance 2t); the constants differ from Austin's accordingly: |f - P_t f|_1 <= sqrt(2t) sum |d_n f|_1, sum |d_n P_t f|_2^2 <= |f|_2^2/(2et), and the final bound 4 sqrt(t) + (2et)^(-a/2) eta^(b/2) with b = tanh(2t/c_0). (4) The bound J is explicit. The general theorem of Austin (compact metric spaces with connected and locally connected support, any modulus of continuity) is not proved; the course proves the case of the interval with a Lipschitz condition, which is what the 106 course uses. No discrepancy with Austin's paper was found in the part that was derived. Checked by the program plan/checks_20261013/hc_check.py: the Gaussian mean of a character; on the circle the sup bound, the bound for mean-zero functions, the inequality with a defect, Rothaus's lemma and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality for 3,000 random functions; hypercontractivity on the circle for 4,000 random functions and times, with a control exponent for which the inequality fails 2,813 times; on the torus of dimension 3 the three inequalities, hypercontractivity and the final bound for 400 random polynomials; the fold map; the numbers of the theorem (q(1) has 163 digits, q(1/10) about 51,000). All parts passed at the first run. Slip stopped before staging: one exercise of the second lesson (6.5) asserted something false (that no inequality with the L^1 norm of the derivative holds); it was replaced by a correct exercise.

open_obligations: The constant 7/4 of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality is not the best one (the best is 1/(2 pi^2), by a theorem of Weissler that the course does not prove). All later exponents and the bound J inherit this loss. The bound J is explicit and very large (log J of the order tau^-4 log(1/tau) for small tau).
Not proved: Austin's theorem in its general form (other spaces and moduli of continuity), and his Theorem 1.3 on maps between Hamming metrics.

Attributions without a checked free reference: the method of the third lesson is attributed to L. Gross and the lemma of the second lesson to O. S. Rothaus from general knowledge; the only source that was read for this course is Austin's paper, which cites Gross, Weissler and Ledoux for the hypercontractive inequality.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
